newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge blasts muni industry at Ferber trial.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge blasts muni industry at Ferber trial.

text.p: U.S. District Judge William Young at Thursday's hearing where he sentenced municipal banker Mark Ferber to 33 months in prison and a $1 million fine took aim at municipal lawyers and underwriters, in particular Merrill Lynch & Co and Lazard Freres & Co.
At one point during his scathing assessment of the industry, the judge likened Ferber's former employer Lazard Freres' attitude to a song sung by a robber in the Broadway hit Les Miserables.
"I saw and heard the most sorry, evasive explication and excuses for legal advice," from municipal bond lawyers during Ferber's trial Young told Ferber, 43, after pronouncing sentence.
"If there had been appropriate legal advice Mr. Ferber, you would not be going to prison," the bespectacled judge, who stands about 5-foot-8 with sandy thinning hair, said from the bench.

The "criminal defense bar has a standard (for ethics and disclosure) that the municipal bond bar would do well to emulate," said the judge, who broke from his characteristic stoic, firm and calm demeanor that he projected througout the trial to lambast the firms.

Ferber, who worked for Lazard Freres, was convicted in August on 58 of 61 counts of fraud and corruption involving a contract he maintained with Merrill Lynch to advise government clients in the municipal bond market. Judge Young dropped 11 of the 58 counts during the first part of the sentencing hearing on Wednesday.

The charges centered on whether or not a contract between Ferber and Merrill Lynch was adequately disclosed to Ferber's government clients including the District of Columbia, the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority and the U.S Postal Service.
Merrill Lynch and Lazard Freres settled with the U.S. Attorney's Office late last year on the matter, paying a total of $24 million in fines with neither firm admitting or denying guilt.
But Young, after questioning Assistant U.S. Attorney Brien O'Connor, noted Merrill Lynch's annual report made no mention of any changes in procedures as a result of its $12 million fine.

"I don't think the $12 million settlement caused them much pain on their way to the tennis courts...and once they understood they had a flawed, unethical character (Ferber) they played him for a patsy," the judge said.

Merrill Lynch spokesman Timothy Gilles said, "We strongly disagree with the judge's characterizations which are unfortunate and unfair. Merrill Lynch's record for integrity and upholding the highest standards of business conduct has been well established over decades."

"We resolved this matter over a year ago to the complete satisfaction of the all law enforcement and regulatory authorities and cooperated fully with the investigation and prosecution of this case," Gilles said.

Young also lashed into Ferber's former employer saying, "Lazard Freres was totally bereft of internal quality controls. Their attitude can be summed up ... by the robber in 'Les Miserables' who sings 'What do I care? Give me my share,'" Young said.
"At least they Lazard Freres had the decency...to get out of the municipal bond businesess," Judge Young said.
Lazard Frere said in a statement, "Lazard has a documented 150-year history of integrity and quality in representing our clients.

"The unauthoritzed activites of a former member of our firm, for which we have paid a heavy price, are highly regrettable: they will in no way change our continued commitment to the qualities that have enabled us to maintain our distinguished position over this long period of time," the firm said.
Ferber, his stocky frame crammed into a blue suit, sat impassively in the court room Thursday morning as the judge railed against the industry.
When asked if had anything to say before the sentence was passed, Ferber, a lawyer who has already been disbarred at the federal level, replied, "I have nothing further to offer the court."

Under a sentencing agreement, Ferber will serve 33 months in prison, have to pay a $1 million fine by Friday afternoon, and was assessed additional penalities of $1,550. In addition, he will have to serve two years of probation.

Prosecutor O'Connor said Ferber would have to serve his the sentence less 115 days for good behavior. Ferber is to report to McKean federal corrections facility, a low security prison near the town of Bradford in northern central Pennsylvania, on Jan. 14.
The $1 million court fine is separate from $650,000 in penalties that the Securities and Exchange Commission leveled against Ferber on Thursday.

In papers filed at the U.S. District Court in Boston, Ferber agreed to settle the charges in the complaint by paying the $650,000 and accepting an order that permanently bars him from the municipal bond industry.
